newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila court all but ends Ramos era.
newsitem.headline: Manila court all but ends Ramos era.

text.p: The Philippine Supreme Court on Tuesday all but killed chances of a second term for President Fidel Ramos by upholding its ban on a petition to change the constitution so he could seek re-election.
Opposition politicians aspiring to run in the May 1998 elections to choose Ramos's successor cheered the ruling which a court spokeswoman said was final.
"It's instant death for Ramos and a mad scramble for 1998," political analyst Nelson Navarro told Reuters.
"Thank God...it would have divided the nation down the line," said opposition senator Edgardo Angara, one of about a dozen politicians aspiring to run in next year's polls.
"Even if Ramos and his crew won...I think he would come out of it with a bloodied presidency," Angara said, adding:
"It's now back to normal."
The constitution, framed in 1987, fixed the president's term at six years without re-election in reaction to the dictatorship under the late Ferdinand Marcos's 20-year rule.
Gloria Macapagal Arroyo, another opposition senator and a leading presidential contender, called the court verdict "a triumph for democracy".

News of the court's decision swept the capital Manila like wildfire and broke only about an hour after visiting Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong said he believed foreign business would welcome a second term for Ramos.

"If you ask foreign investors (if they like) President Ramos to continue for another six years, I think the answer will be yes for the simple reason that you know him and he has done a good job," Goh told a joint news conference with Ramos.
The presidential palace said it was bowing to the court's verdict.
"The Executive Departments respects the decision," Ramos' presidential executive secretary told reporters.
He urged Ramos supporters who initiated the move to amend the constitution to accept the verdict, saying: "This cannot go on endlessly."

The Supreme Court voted 6-6 with two abstentions and one vote discounted to maintain its decision in March disallowing a move by a citizens group to call for a referendum on lifting the term limits of the president and all incumbent officials.
The group has said it has collected almost five million signatures to force the calling of a referendum.

"(The challenge to the decision is) denied with finality, the arguments therein set forth not being of sufficient cogency to persuade the requisite majority of the court to modify or reverse the (original) decision," a court statement said.
About 50 leftists opposed to any constitutional change picketed the court building while the court's justices met.
Ramos has repeatedly denied he has any plans of running for re-election. On Sunday, speaking to businessmen, he pledged a peaceful transfer of power to his successor after the 1998 elections.
"I suspect this is the end of the road for Ramos but I would not bet large amounts of money on it," a Western diplomat said.
"Politics in the Philippines rarely moves in straight lines and there is still a long time left before the elections," he added.
Theoretically, Ramos still has two other options under the law if he wants to change the constitution and run for re-election.
One is to call a constitution convention composed of elected representatives or turn the Congress into a constituent assembly, both of which could initiate constitutional changes.
But analysts said time constraints would rule out such options with the elections barely a year away.
"But I don't think he (Ramos) will do it. It will be an act of madness," analyst Teodoro Benigno told Reuters.
